{{Short description|Convex solid with a continuous, developable surface}}
{{COI|date=September 2020}}
[[File:Sphericon.stl|thumb|[[STL (file format)|STL]] model of a [[sphericon]] ]]

In [[geometry]], a '''developable roller''' is a [[Convex polytope|convex solid]] whose [[Surface (mathematics)|surface]] consists of a single [[Continuous function|continuous]], [[developable surface|developable]] face.<ref name="polycons">{{cite journal |last1=Hirsch |first1=David |title=The Polycons: The Sphericon (or Tetracon) has Found its Family |journal=Journal of Mathematics and the Arts |year=2020 |volume=14 |issue=4 |pages=345–359 |doi=10.1080/17513472.2020.1711651 |url=https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/abs/10.1080/17513472.2020.1711651?journalCode=tmaa20|arxiv=1901.10677 |s2cid=119152692 }}</ref><ref name="Platonicons">{{cite web |last1=Seaton |first1=K. A. |title=Platonicons: The Platonic Solids Start Rolling |url=http://archive.bridgesmathart.org/2020/bridges2020-371.html |publisher=Tessellations Publishing}}</ref> While [[rolling]] on a [[Plane (geometry)|plane]], most developable rollers develop their entire surface so that all the points on the surface touch the rolling plane. All developable rollers have [[ruled surface]]s. Four families of developable rollers have been described to date: the prime poly[[sphericon]]s,<ref name="Polysphericons">{{cite web |title=Polysphericons |url=https://www.h-its.org/projects/polysphericons/ |website=h-its.org |publisher=Heidelberg Institute for Theoretical Studies}}</ref> the [[convex hull|convex hulls]] of the two disc rollers (TDR convex hulls),<ref name="two disc rollers">{{cite web |last1=Ucke |first1=Christian |title=The two-disc-roller — a combination of physics, art and mathematics |url=https://www.ucke.de/christian/physik/ftp/lectures/Wobb3e.pdf |website=Ucke.de}}</ref> the [[polycon]]s <ref name="the polycons">{{cite web |title=Polycons |url=https://www.h-its.org/projects/polycons/ |website=h-it.de |publisher=Heidelberg Institute for Theoretical Studies}}</ref><ref name="polycons"></ref> and the Platonicons.<ref name="Platonicons"></ref><ref name="Platonicons1">{{cite web |title=Platonicons |url=https://2020.bridgesmathart.org/short/371.html |website=2020.bridgesmathart.org |publisher=The Bridges Organization}}</ref>

==Construction==
[[File:comparison_oloid_sphericon_3D.svg|thumb|link={{filepath:comparison_oloid_sphericon_3D.svg}}|Comparison of an oloid (left) and sphericon (right) &mdash; {{nowrap|in [{{filepath:comparison_oloid_sphericon_3D.svg}} the SVG image],}} move over the image to rotate the shapes]]
Each developable roller family is based on a different construction principle. The '''prime polysphericons''' are a subfamily of the [[polysphericon]] family.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Emmer |first1=Michele |title=The visual mind II |date=2005 |publisher=The MIT press |isbn=0-262-05076-5 |page=668-669}}</ref> They are based on bodies made by [[Surface of revolution|rotating]] [[regular polygon|regular polygons]] around one of their longest [[diagonal|diagonals]]. These bodies are cut in two at their symmetry plane and the two halves are reunited after being rotated at an offset angle relative to each other.<ref name="the polycons"></ref> All prime polysphericons have two edges made of one or more circular arcs and four vertices. All of them, but the [[sphericon]], have surfaces that consist of one kind of [[cone|conic]] surface and one, or more, conical or [[cylinder|cylindrical]] [[frustum]] surfaces.<ref name="polycons"></ref> '''Two-disc rollers''' are made of two [[congruence (geometry)|congruent]] symmetrical [[circle|circular]] or [[ellipse|elliptical]] [[circular sector| sectors]]. The sectors are joined to each other such that the planes in which they lie are perpendicular to each other, and their axes of symmetry coincide.<ref name="two disc rollers"></ref> The convex hulls of these structures constitute the members of the TDR convex hull family. All members of this family have two edges (the two circular or elliptical [[arc (geometry)|arcs]]). They may have either 4 [[vertex (geometry) |vertices]], as in the sphericon (which is a member of this family as well) or none, as in the [[oloid]]. Like the prime polysphericons the '''polycons''' are based on regular polygons but consist of identical pieces of only one type of cone with no frustum parts. The cone is created by rotating two adjacent edges of a regular polygon (and in most cases their extensions as well) around the polygon's axis of symmetry that passes through their common vertex. A polycon based on an ''n''-gon (a polygon with n edges) has ''n'' edges and ''n''&nbsp;+&nbsp;2 vertices. The sphericon, which is a member of this family as well, has circular edges. The hexacon's edges are [[parabola|parabolic]]. All other polycons' edges are [[hyperbola|hyperbolic]].<ref name="polycons"></ref> Like the polycons, the '''Platonicons''' are made of only one type of conic surface. Their unique feature is that each one of them circumscribes one of the five [[Platonic solid|Platonic solids]]. Unlike the other families, this family is not infinite. 14 Platonicons have been discovered to date.<ref name="Platonicons"></ref>

==Rolling motion==
Unlike [[Axial symmetry|axially symmetrical]] bodies that, if unrestricted, can perform a [[Linear motion|linear]] [[rolling]] motion (like the [[sphere]] or the cylinder) or a circular one ([[Rolling cone motion|like the cone]]), developable rollers meander while rolling.<ref name="polycons"></ref> Their motion is linear only on average.  In the case of the polycons and Platonicons, as well as some of the prime polysphericons, the path of their [[center of mass]] consists of circular arcs. In the case of the prime polysphericons that have surfaces that contain cylindrical parts the path is a combination of circular arcs and straight lines. A general expression for the shape of the path of the TDR convex hulls center of mass has yet to be derived.<ref name="two disc rollers"></ref>
In order to maintain a smooth rolling motion the center of mass of a rolling body must maintain a constant height. All prime polysphericons, polycons, and platonicons and some of the TDR convex hulls share this property.<ref name="polycons"></ref><ref name="Polysphericons"></ref> Some of the TDR convex hulls, like the oloid, do not possess this property. In order for a TDR convex hull to maintain constant height the following must hold:

: <math>\ c^2=4a^2-2b^2</math>

Where a and b are the half minor and major axes of the elliptic arcs, respectively, and c is the distance between their centers.<ref name="two disc rollers"></ref> For example, in the case where the skeletal structure of the convex hull TDR consists of two circular segments with radius '''r''', for the center of mass to be kept at constant height, the distance between the sectors' centers should be equal to <math>\sqrt{2}</math>'''r'''.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Stewart |first1=A. T. |title=Two-Circle-Roller |journal=American Journal of Physics |year=1966 |volume=34 |issue=2 |pages=166–167 |doi=10.1119/1.1972824 |url=https://aapt.scitation.org/doi/10.1119/1.1972824|url-access=subscription }}</ref>
